title: Has anyone found a stock day trading edge with Claude?
author: Kind-trader
selftext:
Hello, dear traders,

Has anybody been able to produce a significant day trading edge using Claude for day trading stocks that truly works over time? I have generated thousands of strategies with Claude using data from TradingView, but they’re usually overfitted and fail horribly once I provide data from new trading days, even when I ask Claude to avoid overfitting.

I’m just looking for some hope. I don’t expect you to share your strategy.

By a significant trading edge, I mean one that has averaged at least 0.5% per day for at least six months, without astronomical drawdowns or super infrequent trades.

comments.author: lrmcr_rsvd

replies.author: Illustrious_Web_2774

replies.author: lrmcr_rsvd
replies.body: Sure not compundes, but you wont havr that as mean or median

replies.author: moderncharting
replies.body: focus on refining a heavily filtered weekly strategy, they exist if you know the correct questions to ask and have the tools to verify.

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
the thousands of strategies is the problem itself. if you generate a thousand and keep the one that looks best on past data, that one is mostly the luckiest, and new days show it. asking the model to avoid overfitting doesn't help, because the overfitting happens in the picking, not in any single strategy.  
two things that helped me: write the rule down before you look, test it once on data it never saw, and count every version you tried, so the bar goes up with the count. and check the target: 0.5% a day compounded is close to +87% in six months, around 3.5x a year. almost nothing sustains that. a much smaller edge that survives new data is worth more than any of those thousand.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
0.5% a day for six months compounds to close to 90%, a bar almost nobody clears without a big drawdown hiding somewhere, so part of the missing hope is the target.

the bigger problem is the thousands. generate thousands of rules on the same TradingView history and the best few look great by luck alone. telling Claude to avoid overfitting can't fix it, because the overfitting is in the picking, not in any one rule. freeze a few recent months Claude never sees, write down how many rules you tried, and test only the one or two finalists on that chunk, once. if it dies there, it was noise.

I built Quantradin this year for that last step: the rule goes in as plain words, it's tested on past bars with no peeking ahead, and survivors run forward on pretend money before anything real. quantradin.com

what timeframe are the rules on, 1-min or 5-min?

comments.body: I have finally, but I had to spend 3 years building infrastructure for claude to properly go about researching different strategies and portfolios (I don't do black box, 100% deterministic) and with that infrastructure and with proper AI integration, it still took weeks before finding my first edge that held up in unseen periods.

replies.author: Skye_Figer
replies.body: Honestly, I’m still waiting to find out, and it’s too early for me to really claim it. I only have a few months of data showing backtest to paper parity at this time, trade for trade, where fees and slippage are modeled after what paper and live see. The strategy I’m confident with running only trades on average 2/3rds of the year, and really for entries it’s less than that. It’s correctly protected my money the past few months for live, but until the market turns around I won’t truly know. It holds up on data it’s not seen for a number of different time periods, so there’s hope.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Generating thousands of strategies is part of the problem. When you test that many, a few will look great by luck, and they fall apart on new days, which is exactly what you're seeing. Asking Claude to avoid overfitting doesn't fix it, because the filter has to be a test on data it never touched. I'd also question the target, since 0.5% a day compounds to more than triple the account in a year, which is a very high bar. A smaller, steadier goal tested with fees on held-out data is more realistic. Cymetica's Backtest Labs holds out the last part of the history, which suits that kind of check.

comments.author: Interesting-Law-8815
comments.body:
Anyone tell you they have is lying.  

Markets are controlled by massive investment firms with billions of dollars under control.  They spend millions on R&D in order to gain an edge.   Yet random Reddit guy with a $200 Max plan knows something these firms don’t?

They may have struck lucky for a couple of months - maybe their approach has picked up on some small signals used by the Hedge funds - but as soon as signal goes watch them loose that. 

Evidence shows time and time and time again that the best strategy is just buy the market.  You don’t need AI for that.

replies.author: moderncharting
replies.body: you can use the same strategies as them if you know what prompts to ask and have a refined backtesting regime. You have access to essentially the exact same math, research and market history as they do. human emotion doesn't change and statistical realities like standard deviations are cheat codes to finding triggers. a significant amount of edge for all trading strategies is the tried and true worn out adage, cut losers and let winners run. over a large enough timeframe that is the edge to refine. Start there.

comments.author: frylock1666
comments.body:
yeah but leaned heavily into optimization math.... I used to think the challenge was a good strategy but it's not. Its more about being able to figure out how to efficiently optimize a strategy quickly and automatically in such a way that its not curve fitting to one off patterns.... but instead to repeating patterns. That was the hard bit and the piece that isn't really there for now in most commercial systems you can buy.. an LLM isn't well suited to doing it directly but it can help either build the tools or use existing ML tools to do it. One example is boosted trees... another is CMA-ES and so on... they each have different strengths / weaknesses and approaches... one amusing thing though is it was pretty lousy at writing good optimization policies as it would try to be too clever and it just made it harder for the optimizer to search the space.

In terms of profitability... thats largely a function of trading frequency which is a function of data aggregation and where your edge can sit.. its not possible to do high frequency off of daily candles and you'd want a raw tick feed or low aggregation. On the flip side... in terms of how small you can go the limit is really spread etc.... its easier to think of opportunity in terms of multiples of spread.... basically if you bother to build your own optimization framework then you'd want to go intraday trading... it's a lot of work though and a lot of lessons to learn

comments.author: MormonMoron
comments.body:
I have improved performance of our raw signal with it. We have a signal that works pretty well, but is still prone to occasional catastrophe trades. We used Claude to explore a huge subset of input signal variations as the feature engineering step of an LGBM keepout model. 

Today was the first day since we made this keepout live that we have taken a “catastrophe trades” since that got turned on back on 9/21/2026. We are stuck in three trades right now at about -3% (about the same downward motion as the market since open today), but overall we are 6% since 9/21 and our VTI benchmark is -7.5%.

comments.author: Chipware
comments.body:
These AI bots are reactive in nature and they are not good at trading.  They look at the market in snapshots, they do not really understand movement of markets, or combining different data sets like volatility, momentum, decay, etc into a coherent consistently profitable strategy. Basically they are not clever enough to find profitable strategies. However, they can help you refine your strategy by doing the math for you. And help you find the right trades you want but can't do the advanced math as quickly. And they can help you write your own trading app which can interface with your broker's API, and they can help you execute trades pretty well.

I've built my own trading app using Tasty API with AI built into it. I can say things like "Update all shorts stop market to 1.5x current mid" and it will go update 12 positions in 10 seconds.  It would take me about 3 minutes to do that manually.

That's where AI shines in trading, the mechanics.
